latin: Per numeros habetur uia ad omnis scibilis inuestigationem et intellectionem; ad cuius conclusionis uerificationem polliceor me ad infrascriptas xxiii. questiones per uiam numerorum responsurum.
latin_note: The copy-text breaks 'intellectionem' across a line ('in/tellectionem'); the break is repaired here rather than reproduced as a word division (farmer1998:23732).
translation: Through numbers a way is had to the investigation and understanding of everything knowable; and to verify this conclusion I promise to answer the twenty-three questions written below by the way of numbers.
translation_note: 'via' is rendered 'way' rather than more freely as 'method', following Mandosio's argument that the literal rendering is preferable (mandosio2012:166).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch16, from Latin at farmer1998:23732
doctrine: This is the last and most sweeping of the mathematical conclusions in the series, claiming for number a route to the investigation and understanding of everything knowable, and committing Pico to defend the claim through the twenty-three numerical questions that follow it in the text (farmer1998:23732). Farmer calls it one of three or four methods the text credits with leading to knowledge 'of everything knowable', a claim he notes de Lubac denies Pico makes anywhere (farmer1998:23794).
historiography: Wirszubski quotes the conclusion as the last of a series before turning to the Sefer Yetzirah's teaching on the number of ways the world was created, adding no comment of his own beyond the quotation (wirszubski1989:9683). Mandosio quotes the same Latin and argues that via should be translated literally as 'way' rather than more idiomatically as Farmer's 'method' (mandosio2012:166).

quotations.text: quoted, and I shall not add any except the eleventh thesis of Pico's Conclusiones de Mathematicis secundum opinionem propriam
